newsitem.title: THAILAND: Sluggish exports ring alarm bells in Thailand.
newsitem.headline: Sluggish exports ring alarm bells in Thailand.

text.p: Sluggish Thai exports prompted market analysts on Monday to scale down their projections for 1996 national economic growth while the government adopted tax relief measures to boost the battered trade picture.
"Poor exports will have a big impact on gross domestic product (GDP) as they will depress domestic demand for materials and manpower," said economist Somjai Phagaphasvivat of Thammasat University.
Exports accounted for 34 percent of Thailand's 1995 GDP.

Monthly indicators released by the Bank of Thailand (BOT) last Thursday confirmed signs seen since the second quarter that exports, the main engine of growth of the Thai economy since the late 1980s, had lost their previous strength.
BOT data showed exports grew 3.8 percent in January-July against a 26.2 percent rise in the same year-ago period.

Somjai projected the Thai economy, sapped by poor exports, would likely expand 7.2-7.3 percent in 1996. This would be its slowest growth rate in 10 years versus 7.8 percent growth forecast by the BOT and 8.6 percent recorded in 1995.
The economist saw exports rising a maximum six to seven percent for all of 1996 against 10.2 percent projected by the central bank and a 23.6 percent rise in 1995.
Somjai's projection was rosier than that of other analysts.
Olarn Chaipravat, Thai Bankers Association president, said on Friday he expected 1996 exports growth at five percent, the slowest pace since 1984 when Thailand devalued the baht to help exports.
A cabinet economic panel on Friday voted for state agencies to grant a package of tax relief measures to help exporters after acknowledging the 1996 export target would be missed.
Other analysts said the tax measures would take at least a few months to produce any result.

Sriyan Pietrez, chief market strategist at Bangkok Nomura Plc, said he expected sporadic speculation against the baht as long as the market perceived its devaluation as a possible solution for Thai exports.
"Sporadic attacks on the baht may return so long as the market perceives it as a possible remedy for exports," he said.
The Thai central bank intervened in local and regional money markets in late July and early August to defend the baht.
The BOT has warned speculators it would not hesitate to defend the baht with Thailand's $39.4 billion foreign reserves.
Pietrez estimated the BOT had spent $1.8 billion to $2.0 billion in its last round of market intervention.
"Thai foreign reserves may prove not much of a defence if the central bank needs to use them to further defend the baht," he said.
Poor Thai indicators come as Malaysia posted a bullish trade performance, which could prompt foreign funds to adjust regional investment portfolios in favour of Malaysia, he said.

Preecha Jarungidanan, director of Chao Phaya Finance and Securities Co Ltd, said he expected any change in the baht value to be slow, through small and gradual adjustments of the composition of a basket of currencies against which Thailand fixed the baht's daily rate.
"Our economy is not as bad as Mexico's in early 1995. Sluggish exports are a regional phenomenon and our imports have also dropped sharply along with exports," he said.
